paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX1 and her daughters, XXXX XXXX XXXX (XXXX years old) and XXXX XXXX XXXX (XXXX years old),2 citizens of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), are appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rendered on February 3, 2017, rejecting their claim for refugee protection for lack of credibility.

The principal appellant was appointed by the RPD as the designated representative of her two (2) daughters, who were minors at the time.3 In accordance with the Refugee Appeal Division Rules,4 this representative is deemed to have been designated by the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD). However, given that XXXX reached the age of majority during the case, this designation ended on May 9, 2017.5
The appellants did not submit any new evidence in support of their appeal and are not requesting a hearing.
The Minister did not intervene in the appeal.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the determination of the RPD, namely, that the appellants are neither "Convention refugees" nor "persons in need of protection." OVERVIEW AND FACTUAL BACKGROUND OF THE APPEAL
The appellants allege a fear of persecution by reason of the real or imputed political opinion of their spouse/father and because, as women, they are members of a vulnerable social group.

The spouse/father allegedly worked on a special project, XXXX XXXX, from 2013 to 2015. As the minister who had appointed him had fallen out of favour with the party in power, he was allegedly replaced. As a result, the spouse/father was allegedly also replaced and stopped working on the project on XXXX XXXX, 2015.6

The appellants allege that during the night of XXXX XXXX to XXXX, 2015, four (4) armed soldiers showed up at their home looking for information about the XXXX XXXX project; they robbed the spouse/father, taking his computers and work documents. They allegedly promised to come back if they were not satisfied.7
The appellants allege that a complaint was filed the next day.8

The appellants allege that a second incident occurred on XXXX XXXX, 2016, more than a year later. That time, six (6) men showed up during the night-four (4) soldiers and two (2) civilians. Four (4) of them stayed with the spouse/father in the bedroom, while the other two (2) went into the living room with the principal appellant and the children. She was allegedly humiliated in front of her children. The soldiers touched her all over her body, pointed a weapon at her head, and threatened to kill her, her children and her husband. She stated that she was not raped because the other soldiers objected after the husband paid them $600.9 They left, taking belongings with them and threatening to keep coming back because they were looking for important XXXX XXXX project documents.10
The next day, a second complaint was allegedly filed.11

The appellants left the DRC on June 27, 2016, to visit another of the family's children who is studying in Canada. They arrived here the next day.12 The spouse/father came to join them a month later.13

The family was supposed to return to the DRC together on XXXX XXXX, 2016, but the principal appellant decided to stay in Canada with her daughters.14 The couple's relationship had allegedly been strained since the second incident. The spouse/father apparently left and is living in the DRC.
They filed their claim for refugee protection on September 28, 2016.15 ANALYSIS Standard of review
The IRPA does not set out the standard of intervention to be applied by the RAD when reviewing RPD decisions. This standard has been defined by the case law.

In Huruglica,16 the Federal Court of Appeal ruled that the RAD must carry out its own analysis of the record to determine whether, as submitted by the appellant, the RPD erred. With respect to findings of fact (and mixed fact and law) that raised no issue of credibility of oral evidence, the RAD is to review RPD decisions applying the correctness standard.17 This is the standard I will generally apply, with some possible exceptions.

In the case of findings of fact that do raise issues of credibility of oral evidence, the three-member RAD panel18 determined that if the RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage, the RAD will explain how the RPD enjoyed such an advantage, if applicable, and may apply the standard of reasonableness, modified to apply to the RAD context.

In this situation, having listened to the full recording of the hearing, I have no hesitation in concluding that deference is warranted, given the undeniable advantage enjoyed by the RPD, which had the opportunity to observe the appellants and their demeanour at the hearing during any silences and hesitations. By simply listening to the recording, I cannot know if the witnesses are thinking,19 taking the time to read in silence, trying to compose themselves,20 looking at their parent to gauge whether the answers they just gave were appropriate21 or are shaking while testifying.22 Consequently, I will apply the reasonableness standard, modified to apply to the RAD context. RPD decision

The RPD accepted that the spouse/father had indeed worked for the XXXX XXXX project, but it was not satisfied that the rest of the alleged facts had been established.23 It was of the opinion that the various points combined had a sufficiently negative impact on the essential elements in question to find that they had not been established on a balance of probabilities.

According to the RPD, the following points are problematic: * The major contradiction with respect to the date on which the complaint regarding the first home invasion was allegedly filed.24 * The omission in the first complaint of the allegation that the criminals wanted to obtain information regarding the XXXX XXXX project.25 * Their alleged behaviour following the first complaint raised concerns as to the truth of the alleged incident (incident of XXXX XXXX, 2015).26 * The implausibility of the connections made by the principal appellant between the second home invasion and the XXXX XXXX project (recognizing voices, statements not reported in the Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), demeanour during her testimony).27 * The contradictions between the principal appellant's testimony and that of her daughters, as well as between her daughters' testimony and their BOC Form regarding whether the criminals had been masked during the second incident.28 * The contradiction between the principal appellant's testimony and that of her daughters regarding steps taken to protect themselves following the second alleged home invasion (whether or not they returned home).29 * The failure to report the connection between the second home invasion and the XXXX XXXX project in the second complaint.30 * The contradiction between the principal appellant's testimony and the email of XXXX XXXX, 2016, regarding when she found out that there had allegedly been two more night-time visits to their home in the DRC.31 With regard to this same documentary evidence, the RPD noted that the principal appellant had a great deal of difficulty testifying and giving explanations.32 It was not satisfied with the explanations provided to explain the delay between when the new incidents occurred (XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX, 2016) and when the principal appellant was allegedly informed of them by email.33 It noted that the principal appellant did not know whether the criminals had come back once or several times, although the email indicates two new visits and she stated that she had spoken to her husband about the email.34 Lastly, the RPD noted that it took the principal appellant more than two (2) months to communicate this relevant information to her counsel and, ultimately, to the RPD.35

The RPD also noted elements that, individually, would not be determinative but, collectively, reinforce the finding of a lack of credibility, including the following: * The appellant's laboured and contradictory testimony regarding her intentions upon leaving the country, her decision to remain in Canada and her exchanges with her spouse.36 * Her spouse's decision to return to the DRC and stay there despite having a visa permitting him to return to Canada.37

The RPD concluded that the evidence did not establish that her spouse was at risk of persecution. It follows that the appellants did not establish that there is a serious possibility that they would be persecuted by reason of their membership in the particular social group of [translation] "spouse's family members" or by reason of an imputed political opinion (section 96, IRPA).38

The RPD also analyzed their claim under section 97 of the IRPA, namely, whether they would be subjected personally to a danger of torture or to a risk not generally faced by other individuals in the DRC.39 For a number of reasons, the RPD concluded that they had not discharged their burden of proof. The RPD's errors as alleged by the appellants
Essentially, the appellants submit that the RPD decision is wrong in law because it did not take into consideration all of the evidence on the record.40

They submit that the following elements were misinterpreted or improperly assessed: * The appellant's decision not to return to the DRC with her spouse on XXXX XXXX, 2016, and to remain in Canada with her daughters.41 * The date of the first complaint.42 * The failure to mention a connection between the first home invasion and the XXXX XXXX project.43 * The contradiction regarding the return to their home, following the home invasion incident.44 * The statement that it is implausible that the appellant recognized the criminals' voices.45 * The contradiction regarding whether or not the criminals were masked at the time of the second home invasion.46 * The email of XXXX XXXX, 2016.47 * The return to their home following the second incident. * The fact that they are not credible is not a determinative factor, and they should nevertheless be considered refugees if the subjective and objective components are met.48 The appellant's decision not to return to the DRC with her husband on XXXX XXXX, 2016, and to remain in Canada with her daughters

The RPD noted that the appellant's testimony was laboured and contradictory with regard to her intention to leave the country, her decision to remain in Canada and her exchanges with her spouse on these subjects. The RPD took into consideration the sensitive nature of the subject matter in the context of the alleged marital difficulties. Despite this, it found that her answers seemed calculated and that her testimony was not candid.49 In addition, the RPD doubted that her spouse was in danger and that he had to live in hiding, as the appellant claimed, since he had a valid visa for Canada at the time and had returned to work at the Société nationale d'électricité (XXXX) [XXXX XXXX XXXX].50
The appellants argue that the panel misinterpreted their actions (remaining in Canada and letting her spouse return to the DRC alone).

Merely disagreeing with a conclusion of the RPD is not sufficient grounds for me to intervene. The onus is on the appellants to clearly identify in their memorandum references to evidence and the passages where the RPD allegedly erred.51 They do not state how the RPD misinterpreted their decisions and they make no reference to evidence upon which I could rely to draw a contrary conclusion.
I am satisfied, after listening to the recording of the hearing, that each of the points raised and considered by the RPD in coming to this conclusion is based on the evidence.52

I also note the appellant's statement that, when she came to Canada, she did not intend to stay here53 and that she did not discuss her plan to stay here with her spouse.54 In my opinion, this is not consistent with her allegations concerning her subjective fear. The RPD was therefore correct in concluding that this supported its negative finding regarding the principal appellant's credibility. In addition, the RPD wisely weighed this and stated that this factor was not determinative on its own, but simply reinforced the findings already made.55 Date of the first complaint
The RPD noted three (3) different problematic aspects of the appellants' evidence regarding the first home invasion, including the date on which a complaint was filed regarding this incident.56

The RPD noted that the appellant testified that the incident took place during the night of XXXX XXXX to XXXX, 2015, which confirmed what she had written in her BOC Form. Later during the hearing, she stated that she could not recall exactly when she went to the police to file a complaint. The RPD then read her previous statements to her, and she again confirmed that the date of the complaint was XXXX XXXX. The RPD confronted her with the fact that the copy of the complaint submitted into evidence was dated XXXX XXXX. She maintained that she was certain that the complaint had been filed the day after the incident. The RPD was of the opinion that, although the difference was only one or two (2) days, this contradiction had not been explained.57

The appellants submit that the panel made no attempt to understand that the (principal) appellant was in shock after allegedly being assaulted and that it was normal for her not to remember the exact day the complaint was filed. They submit a second argument: that, in the appellant's mind, the next day could just as easily have meant two days later, given that she was deeply shaken.58 According to the appellants, a reasonable person in the same circumstances would conclude that it was misstatement, not a contradiction, taking into account the fact that the appellant was in shock after being sexually assaulted.59
In my opinion, the principal appellant did contradict herself, and did not simply misspeak, as counsel for the appellants would have me believe.

First, I note that the BOC Form is clear with respect to when the complaint was filed-the next day.60 The appellant's initial testimony was also to that effect.61 Then, the RPD sought to clarify exactly what [translation] "the next day" meant for her. She replied [translation] "the day after the assault, the day after they visited us." The RPD again insisted, given that the alleged incident occurred during the night of XXXX XXXX to XXXX, and asked whether for her the next day meant XXXX XXXX. The RPD suggested [translation] "so, it was on XXXX XXXX?" and she hesitated at length before finally replying "I think so, yes." Then, she murmured [translation] "I don't remember the date anymore." After being confronted with the fact that the documentary evidence indicates that the complaint was filed on XXXX XXXX, two (2) days and two (2) nights later, she replied, [translation] "I myself know, I know that my husband filed the complaint the next day."62
My analysis of the evidence leads me to reject the appellants' arguments for three (3) reasons.

First, the appellant's spontaneous point of reference is not the date, but rather the sequence of events: she stated that one night the assault occurred and the next day the complaint was filed. In either scenario, as the RPD rightly suggested, this would mean that the complaint would have been filed on either XXXX XXXX or XXXX XXXX, but not on XXXX XXXX. Yet, the documentary evidence submitted by the appellants indicates that it was filed on XXXX XXXX.63

Second, contrary to what the appellants argue in their memorandum, at no time did the appellant testify that for her [translation] "the next day" could also mean two (2) days later. I therefore have no evidence to support such an interpretation.

Third, when explaining what she meant by "the next day," the appellant spontaneously referred to [translation] "the assault." However, according to the evidence, the assault did not occur during the first home invasion incident, but rather during the second.64

In my opinion, the RPD thoroughly canvassed this aspect of the evidence and gave the appellant every opportunity to clarify this contradiction in her evidence. The RPD drew a negative inference as to her credibility.
I am of the opinion that the RPD properly assessed all of the evidence on this point. Failure to mention a connection between the first home invasion incident and the XXXX XXXX project

The RPD noted that, although the appellants insisted that there was a connection between the spouse's involvement in the XXXX XXXX project and the first home invasion in their BOC Form and in their testimony, there is no mention of this in the complaint they allegedly submitted. The RPD found it unreasonable that, as the appellant suggested, the police would have failed to note this important connection, had they been informed of it. It also found it unreasonable that the spouse would have signed the complaint after noticing that a key element was missing.65

In their memorandum, the appellants submit that they did not allege that the complaint was filed by the principal appellant (the mother) and, therefore, there is no way she could have known exactly what her husband told the police because she was not with him at the police station.66 They argue that they are certain that the spouse/father would have disclosed this [translation] "detail" to the police and that the police must not have made note of it.

I agree with the RPD that the appellants' argument means that they are claiming that the spouse signed a complaint that was incomplete with respect to a key aspect of the incident, namely, the motive for the crime. Contrary to the appellants' argument, I am of the opinion that this is not a detail but a key aspect of this home invasion and the theft of the particular property that was taken.

In addition, the appellant testified that she had personally accompanied her spouse when the first complaint was filed, but that he had done all the talking, while she went in and out of the room.67 She testified [translation] "that she believed he had explained" (the reasons why the criminals came to the house).68 The RPD patiently tried to verify whether the information had been given to the police. The RPD understood the concern as it even reformulated a question, stating [translation] "if my husband had told everything?" and she then replied [translation] "that they talked a great deal more about the burglary," and then added "I believe it was mentioned. I do not remember."69 The RPD confronted her, as it should in such circumstances, and she explained [translation] "personally, I do not know why they did not make note of it. That is what we were all saying."70 Yet, the appellant clearly stated that only her spouse had spoken when the complaint was filed, as she was an [translation] "onlooker."

At no time did she provide an explanation for how her husband could have ignored such an important aspect of this first incident, especially given the criminals' alleged threat to return if they did not find what they were looking for.71
The RPD noted that, in the circumstances, without this detail, the complaint simply recounts a random theft, not the circumstances put forward by the appellants.
I am of the opinion that the RPD properly assessed the evidence. The contradiction regarding the return to their home following the home invasion

The RPD was of the opinion that the fact that they remained at the home, stated that life went on and took a return trip to Canada (without claiming refugee protection) does not show that they took any steps to mitigate or eliminate the alleged risks.72

The appellants allege that the RPD erred in its analysis and that their behaviour was consistent because the appellant had explained that thefts are commonplace in the DRC. They add that they initially sought refuge with a friend and that it would be absurd and unthinkable for them to be able to stay there forever.73

The appellants have misunderstood the RPD's statements, which explicitly refer to the first incident, as the subheading in its decision indicates.74 First, the appellants argue that thefts are commonplace in the DRC, which the principal appellant indeed stated during her testimony describing the steps they took following the first incident.75 She testified that the only step they took was to file a complaint at that time. Then, the appellants reiterate that they sought refuge with a friend and that they could not stay there forever. Yet, the recording of the hearing reveals that they sought refuge with the appellant's parents, not with a friend, and that they did so after the second incident, not the first.

In the circumstances, I am of the opinion that the appellants have failed to persuade me that the RPD erred on this point. In my opinion, the RPD's finding here is correct. The finding that it is implausible that the appellant recognized the criminals' voices

The RPD asked the appellant what had led her to make a connection between the second incident and the XXXX XXXX project, and it was not satisfied with her answers for two (2) reasons. First, the appellant stated that she had recognized the criminals' voices, but she had not mentioned this important detail anywhere else, such as in her BOC Form.76 The RPD noted that her entire testimony on a key element of her story had a negative impact on the assessment of her testimony, given that it was implausible that she would remember the voices, given the traumatic nature of the alleged incidents and the time that had elapsed between the two (2) incidents (over a year), and considered that this was a significant omission. In addition, when the RPD confronted her to give her the opportunity to offer an explanation, her testimony became strained, evasive, contradictory and hesitant.77

The appellants criticize the RPD for concluding that it was implausible that she (the principal appellant) would be able to remember the criminals' voices. They argue that there are voices that are hard to forget, that can be remembered our entire lives, especially when those voices are traumatizing and horrible.78

I note that the appellants are not challenging the omission noted by the RPD, namely, the appellant's failure to mention this means of identification. It must be kept in mind that this was, according to her, the connection between the second home invasion and the XXXX XXXX project. If I were to agree with the appellants' argument (that it is plausible that she remembered the voices), that would be all the more reason why she should have disclosed this fact long before her testimony. In my humble opinion, this is a significant omission that undermines her credibility. As a result, the RPD's finding regarding the implausibility of remembering voices becomes very much secondary.

In the circumstances, I reject this argument because whether they are right or wrong does not change the fact that it should have been disclosed when she completed her BOC Form. Contradiction regarding whether or not the criminals were masked at the time of the second home invasion

The RPD found that the children's testimony reinforced its doubts as to the credibility of their allegations. They contradicted themselves (BOC Form versus testimony) and each other (testimony of the children versus that of their mother) when they stated that they had seen the criminals' faces when, up to that point, the evidence was that the men had all been masked.79
The appellants criticize the RPD for focusing on a minor detail and argue that it would be difficult even for an adult to accurately state whether the criminals had been masked or not.80

I am mindful that testifying is stressful for any person claiming refugee protection, let alone a child. But in the appellants' case, these are not young children. They were 17 and 15 years old, respectively, at the time of the alleged events and the hearing.

I understand that it would be difficult for children to accurately describe faces seen in the dark, in the stressful context of a home invasion. However, what is at issue is not the accuracy of the description of the criminals' faces. Therefore, I disagree with the appellants' argument.
The children did not testify that they were not sure whether they had seen the criminals' faces. One cannot simply put forward speculation: statements must be tied to the evidence.
XXXX stated that she had seen the faces of two (2) of the men who were there.
XXXX testified that she had nothing to add to her sister's testimony. She did not correct her sister's testimony. She stated, however, that she saw three (3) or four (4) men.81

I note that they were not very talkative or spontaneous. They were unable to describe the criminals, even in general terms (young or old). They did not mention how they were dressed. Ultimately, the only information obtained by means of a series of questions increasingly led by the RPD was that they were men, they were black, and that the girls did not know them, would not recognize them and had seen their faces.

They contradicted their mother and their BOC Form. The principal appellant testified in her daughters' absence, at her request and with the agreement of all.82 They did not hear the account given earlier by their mother. The RPD also noted that the girls looked to their mother for approval later during their testimony.83 Seeing that her daughters were providing information that differed from her testimony, the principal appellant intervened and the RPD had to reframe things to enable the children to say what they had to say.
I find that the RPD correctly assessed the children's credibility. Email of September 29, 2016

The RPD concluded that the email the appellant received from her spouse on XXXX XXXX, 2016, had no probative value for several reasons. First, because the appellant's testimony regarding the new incidents described in this email and when she learned of them was strained, hesitant and evasive.84 Second, because she contradicted herself regarding the content, as she stated that she had learned that these new incidents had occurred upon receiving the email, whereas in the email, her spouse states, [translation] "as I told you on the telephone."85 Third, because her spouse apparently waited until XXXX XXXX, 2016, to inform the appellant of incidents that occurred on XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX, 2016, although they were in contact with each other and he knew that the appellants had filed a claim for refugee protection.86 Fourth, because the appellant did not know whether the criminals had come more than once, although she stated that she had discussed the email, which indicates that there were two (2) incidents, with her spouse.87 Fifth, because the appellant did not report these new incidents until the hearing and allegedly forgot to disclose the information to her own counsel prior to the day before the hearing.88
The RPD considered that this was an attempt to mislead the panel.89

The appellants argue that the RPD erred in its analysis. They acknowledge that there is a contradiction in the appellant's allegations concerning her statement that she had not heard from her spouse. However, they submit that the RPD failed to consider that the couple's relationship was rocky, since he had left in anger when the appellant told him that she did not intend to return to the DRC, which further explains the lack of communication.90 They add that the fact that the email states [translation] "as I told you on the telephone" does not prove that her spouse had told the appellant on the telephone that the criminals had returned.

I cannot accept the appellants' first argument, as the RPD explicitly considered all of the appellant's allegations to explain the difficult situation with her spouse-specifically, the incidents themselves, her decision not to return to her country and her suspicions that her husband was having an affair.91

I cannot accept the second argument either, as it would mean precisely the opposite of what is stated in the email. According to this email, the only information that was not communicated by telephone was the fact that these events had driven her spouse to leave the house. Indeed, the email states, [translation] "I did not tell you that this has driven me to leave the house. I am currently staying with cousin XXXX in Kimbangu."92
Ultimately, the RPD correctly assessed the probative value of this evidence. I agree with the RPD's conclusion that it has no probative value. Return to their home following the second incident

The RPD noted that there was a contradiction in the appellants' evidence regarding what steps they took following the second home invasion, which allegedly occurred on XXXX XXXX, 2016. The children contradicted their mother's testimony and they were hesitant, looking to her to gauge her reaction.93 The RPD gave the appellant the opportunity to comment on her daughters' testimony, and she again gave an evasive and contradictory testimony.
The appellants state that the RPD misread and misinterpreted the facts. They argue that it would be absurd for the children to be able to count these days or recite them like a lesson.
I do not agree with the appellants' arguments.

The RPD did not ask the children how many days they spent away from their home. It wanted to know whether or not they had returned to the house. The RPD was assessing the consistency between their alleged subjective fear and their behaviour.

A review of the recording reveals, beyond a shadow of a doubt, the contradictions in this portion of the evidence: * The principal appellant initially testified that the day after the second home invasion, she took the children and went to stay with her parents for a few days.94 She stated that after a few days, [translation] "I returned home."95 * The children, on the other hand, testified that they had not returned home after XXXX XXXX.96 They allegedly stayed at the home of one of their mother's friends.97 * Their mother then commented on their testimony and stated that, [translation] "Sometimes the girls came there, sometimes they did not. They came to the house twice. To sleep, like that, they did not come."98 * Their mother then stated that, [translation] "Yes, they slept at home."99

In the circumstances, I am of the opinion that the RPD's finding, that they had not credibly established that their behaviour was consistent with the seriousness of the situation alleged in their story, is founded. The appellants have not persuaded me otherwise. The fact that they are not credible is not a determinative factor and they should nevertheless be considered refugees if the subjective and objective components are met

The RPD concluded that the appellants had not established that they were the victims of a home invasion in their country in the past or that that they would face a serious possibility of persecution in the future by reason of their membership in the particular social group of [translation] "spouse's family members / imputed political opinion" or by reason of their membership in the particular social group of [translation] "women."100
The appellants submit that they must be considered refugees whether they are credible or not, as long as they meet the subjective and objective components for being granted refugee status.101

According to the case law, it is true that both the subjective and objective components are necessary to satisfy the requirements of section 96 of the Act.102 However, a conclusion that a claimant's subjective fear is not objectively well founded is fatal to the determination of Convention refugee status.103

The RPD was of the opinion that the appellants had not established that the Congolese authorities had a particular interest in them. Furthermore, the RPD took into consideration their family and social situation and concluded that they had not established that the overall crime rate in the DRC would make the risk of a sexual or other type of assault more than a mere possibility for them.104
The appellants submit that the RPD did not take all of the evidence into consideration.
Having conducted an independent analysis, I conclude that the RPD considered all the required elements. In addition, I am of the opinion that it properly assessed and weighed all of the evidence.
Consequently, I am of the opinion that the appellants have not discharged their burden of proof on appeal.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, I dismiss the appeal and confirm the RPD's determination.
